newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech govt agrees cabinet changes, recovery steps.
newsitem.headline: Czech govt agrees cabinet changes, recovery steps.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said his government, severely criticised for its handling of a worsening economic situation, agreed on Wednesday on a recovery programme and changes to the cabinet.
The agreement, reached after a six-hour meeting of the three partners in the coalition, meant the centre-right government would stay in power but with several key ministerial changes.
"We reached an agreement...As you know, it gave us a lot of work. We believe this agreement is a step forward," Klaus told a news conference.

Klaus, a monetarist economist who has headed the government since 1993, said the recovery programme included spending cuts, public sector wage freezes, restrictions on imports and unspecified steps to support the central bank's tight monetary policy.
He said the programme was painful but the fastest way to growth in the future. In the meantime, the price would be higher inflation, more unemployment, lower wages and a fall in economic output.

The agreement follows 10 turbulent days of severe speculative pressure on the Czech crown which culminated in the Czech National Bank (CNB) giving in to the speculative selling pressure and allowing the currency to float.

"The retreat from the overvalued exchange rate of the crown, whose value did not correspond to the real effectiveness of our economy, is the reckoning for a number of mistakes in economic policy," Klaus said.
The premier said Education Minister Ivan Pilip would take over the key post of finance minister and current Czech ambassador to Britain Karel Kuhnl would be the new Industry and Trade Minister.
Pavel Necas would be the new Interior Minister and Jiri Grusa would take the education portfolio.

The three coalition partners agreed last week to make cabinet changes with the government's popularity showing a sharp drop sparked by an economic downturn and several high-profile financial scandals.
However, some critics had been calling for the whole government, which has been riven by internal dissent in recent weeks, to resign.
The new programme is meant to back up a package of measures intended to kick-start the economy and combat economic crime, announced in April.

The long-drawn-out negotiations on the new cabinet have been closely watched by the foreign exchange markets, especially since the central bank's decision to scrap the bands within which the crown was allowed to fluctuate against a currency basket made up of the German mark and U.S. dollar.
Pressure to sell the crown grew as investors became increasingly alarmed at widening trade and current account deficits and at the growing uncertainty over the fate of the government.

The Czech Republic, which became a sovereign state in 1993 when Czechoslovakia split, enjoyed several years of demand led growth. But industrial output has declined recently, contributing to the trade deficit.
